items.english: It is a heat such as has not been known in recent years. Whichever way you look, the roof-tiles of the mud-plastered houses throw back the sunlight dully, like lead, and even the swallows' nests hung beneath them, at this rate, look to steam their chicks and eggs to death where they lie. Still more, every field that is a field, whether hemp or millet, has bowed its head limply in the earth-steam, and not one thing keeps its green unwilted. The sky seen above those fields, perhaps stricken by the damp heat of these past days, is turbid and clouded near the ground though it is fine, and here and there the cloud-peaks float in drops, mere shapes, like hail parched in a roasting pan. — The tale of the "wine worm" begins with three men who have gone out of their way to come into a threshing ground in the blazing sun, in such weather.
notes: Kept the hail-parched-in-a-pan simile baldly as in the Japanese; it is meant to look forced and learned.

items.english: Strangely, one of them lies stark naked, face upward on the bare ground. What is more, for some reason his hands and his feet are wound round and round with thin cord. Yet the man himself shows no particular sign of minding it. He is short, fresh-complexioned, somehow giving an impression of dull heaviness, a man fat as a pig. Then a handy unglazed jar stands at this man's pillow, but what may be inside that, too, is not known.

Another is a monk of strange and ancient visage at first sight, in a yellow robe with a small bronze ring hanging from his ear. His skin is black beyond the common, and to see his hair and beard all curled, he would seem a man come from somewhere west of the Onion Ranges. Until now he has patiently waved a fly-whisk with a red handle, driving from the naked man the horseflies and flies that would settle on him, but as might be expected looking a little tired, he has now come beside that same unglazed jar and squats there solemnly, in the posture of a turkey.
notes: Onion Ranges renders Sourrei in the text's own period geography for the Pamirs; fly-whisk renders shubi, the monk's horsehair whisk, in line without further gloss.

items.english: The last one stands far apart from these two, under the eaves of a thatched hut in the corner of the threshing ground. This man grows on the tip of his chin a merely formal beard like a rat's tail, and his rig is a soap-black cloth gown long enough to hide his heels, with a tea-brown sash whose knot hangs slovenly down. Judging by the way he now and then uses with care a fan made of white bird feathers, he is most likely a Confucian scholar or something of the sort.

These three men, all three as if by agreement, hold their tongues. Moreover they scarcely so much as stir, so that you would think they take an extraordinary interest in something about to happen, and for that are all holding their breath.

The sun must be exactly at midday. Perhaps because even the dogs are napping, not a single bark is heard. The hemp and millet hemming the threshing ground gloss their green leaves in the sun and rest hushed and utterly still. And then the sky seen beyond them drifts everywhere oppressively with shimmering haze, so that you suspect even the cloud-peaks are panting in this drought. As far as the eye reaches, nothing seems to breathe but these three men. And those three, again, keep their silence like the clay images enshrined in a Lord Guan temple....
Of course, this is no tale of Japan. — It is an event that happened one summer on the threshing ground of the Liu family at a place called Chozan in China.

data.say: Drafted the opening tableau in a present-tense freeze, keeping heat, threshing ground, jar, and period terms stable.
